👍Commissioner candidates pledged to continue Europe’s green and just transition, lowering energy bills and moving away from fossil fuels. Their focus will be on clean industry leadership, expanding renewables, upgrading grids, accelerating electrification, and addressing climate impacts. 🧵3/9

💥The new political balance in the EU institutions herald a cycle making green policies more contentious. Teresa Ribera's hearing (transition portfolio) was the most tense of all. The Commission - and its climate agenda - is still supported by Christian-democrats, liberals, and social-democrats, giving it a strong political foundation. But this coalition's leadership may struggle as right-wing-only majorities in the Parliament, Commission, and Council become more viable. 🧵8/9

This dynamic risks aggravating mistrust and polarisation, leading to institutional clashes, policy inconsistencies, and ultimately inaction and paralysis. Yet, the EU’s effective response to pressing geopolitical and climate challenges still depends on its ability to build unity and consensus. 🧵9/9

USA basins such as Permian, one of the most productive oil & gas basins in the world, is leaking methane to the tune of 9x to 14x the industry limit — nearly 640,000 lbs/hr. Methane pollution has long been underestimated & not well-understood, and yet natural gas — which is up to 90% methane — is rising as the fossil fuel of choice to generate electricity. What scientists do know is that methane traps 80x as much heat as carbon dioxide in its first 20 atmospheric years.

The satellite’s early reports are staggering. Half a million wells producing just 7% of US oil & gas generate 50% of the industry’s methane pollution. Satellite data from major oil producing countries Turkmenistan & Venezuela shows the problem is particularly severe with one basin at 970,000 lbs/hr.

MethaneSAT also produced the first images of methane emissions from Venezuela, a South American petrostate with the world’s largest oil reserves. But because of Venezuela’s proximity to the tropics and frequent cloud cover, capturing its methane emissions has proved challenging.

Tackling methane emissions has great potential to ease the pace of the climate crisis & cutting methane pollution makes the oil and gas industry “the ‘low-hanging fruit’ of methane mitigation. But the climate crisis still needs an actual solution – which is to stop using fossil fuels altogether.

Happily jumbling correlation with causation, the Telegraph and Wright claim that falling primary energy use shows net zero is bad for the economy. There's just one teeny, tiny problem with this argument: primary energy use has been falling globally, thanks to rising efficiency.

Needless to say, linking the UK's poor economic and social conditions to net zero is propagandistic sleight of hand. Beyond weak, high-school-level correlative arguments, there is no evidence that net zero policies have harmed the UK's economic performance, and I challenge anyone to produce any.

After all, every major economy on Earth has now committed to achieving net zero, and the UK is no longer a frontrunner in pursuing that goal. The UK has fallen behind in the green transition which, according to economists, *is* the economy of the future.

COP29 ended, as it began, in controversy. The main target of that controversy shifted over the course of COP29’s trajectory. At the outset the focus was the selection of Azerbaijan as host and what could realistically be expected from its climate leadership.

But by the end of COP29 concerns about greenwashing gave way to concerns about what had, and had not, been agreed as the conference’s final outcome. The existence of an agreement precludes, for now, dismissal of COP29 as a failure.

Despite international furor about greenwashing and exaltation of fossil fuels, Azerbaijan will be very satisfied with COP29. The event gave a counterpoint to the international conversation about ethnic cleansing, demonstrated event capacity for more than Eurovision, Formula 1 and European Games.

If COP29 is eventually deemed a failure due to the sparseness of financing for transitions to renewables, it will be quite some time before that conclusion can definitively be reached, and if it is, richer countries of the Global North, many of them former colonial powers, can be held responsible.

Azerbaijan’s leadership used the platform afforded by COP29 to prefigure such arguments and give some of Azerbaijan’s bêtes noires a good dressing down in another assertion of Azerbaijan's self-distancing from the West.

There are two clear losers in COP29. The first is the poorer countries at the hard edge of climate change, who in the hard-won commitments to inadequate financing of their energy transitions see a global betrayal.

The other is the cause of peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan. While feverish speculation about a possible peace agreement before or at COP29 was misplaced, no confidence-building gestures or agreements were reached around the conference, pitched by Azerbaijan to the world as a ‘peace COP’.

🌎 The business value of measuring and reducing carbon emissions

Understanding and addressing carbon emissions is an essential aspect of modern business operations. Emissions are categorized into three scopes, each representing different parts of an organization’s value chain.

Accurately measuring emissions across these scopes allows organisations to identify climate, financial, and regulatory risks. This enables businesses to proactively address challenges, align with evolving regulations, and mitigate exposure to potential liabilities.

Measurement also provides a foundation for setting reduction targets and tracking progress toward achieving sustainability goals.

Reducing emissions creates opportunities for operational efficiency and cost savings.

Integrating emissions reduction strategies into business models supports long-term competitiveness. In a low-carbon economy, organizations that lead in decarbonization can distinguish themselves from competitors.

Investors increasingly prioritize sustainability performance in their decision-making, and employees value alignment with organizational values. A credible approach to emissions reduction can enhance investor confidence, improve employee engagement, and secure a stronger social license to operate.

Measuring and reducing carbon emissions is not solely a regulatory or environmental imperative—it is a strategic business opportunity. Organisations that integrate these practices into their core operations can reduce risks, embed efficiency gains, ...

... and position themselves for success in a rapidly evolving economic and environmental landscape.

Is carbon neutral dead? Not yet, but it should be. 

The established corporate practice over the last few years: measuring and reducing emissions and then buying carbon credits to make a compensation claim (like carbon neutral) is being overtaken.

It has now become well understood that carbon neutral represents something of (1) a shortcut (it doesn't cover the full emissions of an organisation), (2) gives a false impression to stakeholders (all companies are on a journey to net zero, no company is able yet to make such an absolute claim)
and (3) is a huge reputational risk (most carbon credits do not deliver the metric tonne of carbon promised, leading to greenwash risk for any organisation relying on them).

The new, higher impact and lower risk approach - contribution claims under a beyond value chain mitigation (BVCM) model - is now increasingly accepted as the best practice approach to companies funding climate projects outside of their value chain.

WWF's recently published report is the latest to set out clearly that BVCM models are required for any organisation seeking to be a climate leader.

Here are the some (not all...for a failed attempt at brevity) of the key principles WWF recommends:

- Companies must first reduce their value chain emissions in line with a 1.5ºC pathway
- Companies should contribute to climate mitigation beyond their value chains 
- Companies should not offset or substitute required emission reductions, and should shift to a contribution approach

-Buyers should not use carbon credits to offset or substitute required emission reductions but can use carbon credits within their BVCM portfolio with a contribution claim
- Projects should enhance biodiversity and deliver social benefits, alongside climate mitigation

(end)
